title: Eksoskalaton: Design, Control, and Evaluation of an Assistive Lower-Limb Exoskeleton Robot

authors.name: Dr. R. Hidayat
authors.affiliation: Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: We propose Eksoskalaton, a novel approach to the design and control of an assistive lower-limb exoskeleton robot tailored for gait assistance and rehabilitation. Existing exoskeleton systems either focus on high-power industrial assistance or clinically oriented rehabilitation devices that lack real-time adaptability; despite achieving reasonable assistance torques, prior work suffers from limited closed-loop human-in-the-loop safety measures and communication latency that prevents robust real-time control [1][2][3]. The proposed Eksoskalaton system is designed to integrate a hybrid Model Predictive Control (MPC)-PID cascade, redundant sensor fusion (IMU, high-resolution encoders, force sensors), and a hard real-time EtherCAT backbone to deliver low latency $<$20 ms control with energy-efficient actuation. Extensive experiments on a laboratory prototype show that our method achieves 95.4% tracking accuracy and reduces energy per gait cycle by 28.7% compared to MPC baselines, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in latency and endurance. The system also demonstrates reliable endurance over 1000 cycles with joint drift limited to 3.12 deg. The main contributions of this work are: (1) the Eksoskalaton hardware and actuator architecture optimized for ambulatory assistance; (2) a hybrid MPC-PID control strategy for real-time adaptive assistance; (3) a communication and safety pipeline enabling sub-20 ms closed-loop performance; and (4) a comprehensive experimental validation including endurance and comparative benchmarks. The proposed Eksoskalaton advances practical exoskeleton deployment for assistive robotics and rehabilitation settings.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Human mobility assistance using powered exoskeletons has the potential to transform rehabilitation, eldercare, and industrial augmentation. In particular, lower-limb exoskeletons can restore gait for individuals with mobility impairment and augment walking endurance for industrial operators. The field has matured rapidly with improvements in actuation, sensing, and control algorithms, yet practical deployment is hindered by constraints including battery energy density, real-time control latency, safety under human contact, and seamless human-in-the-loop intention decoding. Addressing these practical engineering constraints is essential to translate lab prototypes into robust, field-ready systems that meet clinical and industrial requirements.

Prior work in exoskeleton robotics has explored a broad space of designs and control methods. Several clinically oriented systems emphasize compliant actuation and user safety but sacrifice dynamic performance [1][4][5]. Industrial exoskeletons focus on high torque and ruggedness, yet they often neglect precise gait coordination and closed-loop sensing that accounts for human intent [2][6]. Control methods range from simple assist-as-needed PID loops to sophisticated optimal controllers such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) and learning-based policies [7][8][9]. Despite achieving competitive trajectory tracking or energy savings, prior work suffers from limitations in communication determinism and sensor redundancy, which reduce robustness in real-world deployments. It is worth noting that systems relying solely on wireless telemetry or high-latency networks cannot guarantee the sub-20 ms reaction times often required for safe human-exoskeleton interaction.

The problem we address is the integrated design of an assistive lower-limb exoskeleton, named Eksoskalaton, that provides robust, low-latency assistance while maintaining safety, energy efficiency, and clinical relevance. The research gap spans hardware (actuator-packing, battery integration), real-time communication (EtherCAT versus CAN), and control (hybrid MPC-PID cascades that trade off optimality and computational feasibility). To address this challenge, we introduce Eksoskalaton, a system that combines a modular hardware layout, redundant sensing and sensor fusion, a hierarchical control architecture, and deterministic communication to meet stringent latency and safety metrics.

We propose Eksoskalaton, a novel approach to the exoskeleton problem. The proposed system is designed to: 

 The main contributions of this work are:

1) A practical hardware architecture for a lower-limb exoskeleton integrating four torque-capable actuators, a 48V battery pack, and embedded motor drivers optimized for energy efficiency and thermal management.
2) A hybrid control strategy combining MPC for trajectory-level optimization and PID loops for joint-level stability, enabling low-latency response while retaining predictive benefits.
3) A sensor fusion pipeline combining IMU, encoder, and force sensor data with a Kalman-based estimator and fail-safe redundancy.
4) A deterministic communication and safety framework using EtherCAT and CAN with explicit latency budgets and watchdog mechanisms.
5) Extensive experimental validation including tracking accuracy, energy per gait cycle, endurance over 1000 cycles, and a comparison to state-of-the-art baselines.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on exoskeleton hardware, control, and communication protocols. Section III presents the Eksoskalaton system architecture, hardware configuration, and detailed control algorithms. Section IV describes the experimental setup and presents quantitative results including performance comparison and endurance testing. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future work directions.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section provides a focused review of the literature in three complementary areas: exoskeleton hardware architectures, control strategies for human-robot gait assistance, and communication and safety frameworks for wearable robots. The survey emphasizes recent advances and persistent limitations in state-of-the-art systems, motivating the design choices of Eksoskalaton.

content.text: Over the past decade engineers have explored diverse mechanical designs for lower-limb exoskeletons. Early systems emphasized rigid braces and high torque motors to deliver support during sit-to-stand and industrial lifting tasks [10][11]. Later works introduced series elastic actuators and quasi-direct drive motors to improve compliance and energy efficiency [12][13][14]. For example, the device in [12] uses series elasticity to decouple actuator inertia from human joints, improving safety under impact, but this choice increases control complexity and reduces peak bandwidth. Conversely, designs that prioritize compact power density, such as quasi-direct drive actuators, achieve higher bandwidth at the cost of greater thermal dissipation and cooling needs [15]. Across these studies, common limitations include limited battery integration for ambulatory use, insufficient modularity for multi-joint assistance, and incomplete attention to cable routing and human ergonomics. Eksoskalaton adopts a hybrid approach with torque-dense brushless motors, compact planetary gear stages for torque multiplication, and thermal-aware mounting to balance bandwidth and endurance.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the Eksoskalaton mechanical layout balances torque capability and ergonomic considerations. The prototype uses compact actuator modules at hip and knee with lighter units at the ankle. We selected brushless motors with planetary gearboxes and incorporated current shunt sensing at each driver to enable closed-loop torque estimation. It is worth noting that actuator selection impacts thermal design and battery sizing directly, which motivated our choice of a 48V, 10Ah battery pack to support extended testing without excessive weight penalty.

Control of wearable robots must reconcile human biomechanics, unpredictable disturbances, and the need for safe interactions. Classic approaches use PID controllers around joint-level torque loops for simplicity and robustness [16]. More advanced controllers employ model-based techniques such as LQR and MPC to account for dynamic coupling and constraints [7][17][18]. MPC offers constraint handling and anticipatory behavior but is computationally heavier, often requiring predictive horizons tuned to trade off optimality and latency. Hybrid cascaded strategies combine an MPC layer for trajectory generation with local PID or impedance controllers for fast inner loops; this combination is effective in maintaining real-time responsiveness while benefiting from model-based planning [8][19]. Learning-based methods, including reinforcement learning and iterative learning control, have been applied to adapt assistance profiles to individual users, but they often demand large datasets and cautious safety verification before human trials [9][20].

Despite the strengths of MPC and learning-based methods, prior work suffers from limitations: high computational cost that increases latency, sensitivity to model mismatch, and limited integration with deterministic communication networks required for wearable safety. To address these gaps, Eksoskalaton integrates a short-horizon MPC with a fast PID cascade, supported by a state estimator that reduces model mismatch by fusing sensor streams.

Reliable communication and explicit safety layers are essential in exoskeleton systems. Protocols such as EtherCAT provide deterministic real-time performance that is well suited for multi-node joint control [21][22]. CAN remains widely used for diagnostics and lower-rate sensor networks due to its robustness and simplicity [23]. Prior implementations that relied on non-deterministic wireless links experienced unacceptable jitter in closed-loop control, reducing stability margins [24]. Safety frameworks often include hardware watchdogs, torque limits, and redundancy in sensing for fault detection; however, designs commonly omit explicit latency budgets for each pipeline stage, making it difficult to certify system behavior under worst-case conditions [25][26].

Eksoskalaton addresses these issues by adopting EtherCAT for joint real-time control, CAN for peripheral sensors and diagnostics, and a software watchdog hierarchy coordinated by the main real-time controller. We also include a human-interface emergency stop and multiple layers of hardware interlocks to protect the user during anomalous conditions. This combination of deterministic communication and multi-level safety is central to enabling sub-20 ms closed-loop control while maintaining robust operation in laboratory and clinical settings.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the Eksoskalaton architecture, hardware configuration, algorithmic design, and communication pipeline. We present mathematical models, controller formulations, and safety procedures. The proposed module-level design is aimed at modularity, real-time determinism, and energy efficiency.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of layered modules: sensors, sensor fusion and state estimation, trajectory planner, hybrid MPC-PID controller, motor drivers, power management, and human interface. The sensor layer comprises high-resolution absolute encoders at each joint, an IMU on the torso, and force sensors at foot interfaces. Sensor data are timestamped and forwarded over a CAN bus to the real-time controller and over EtherCAT to Joint Control Nodes. The state estimator produces a fused state $\hat{x}$ that feeds the trajectory planner which outputs desired joint references $q_{ref}(t)$. The predictive layer computes optimal torque commands $\tau_{opt}$ subject to actuator and safety constraints, while the low-level PID layer ensures fast torque tracking and disturbance rejection. The proposed module-based architecture is designed to permit incremental upgrades: additional sensors, more advanced predictive layers, or cloud telemetry can be integrated with minimal architectural changes.

content.Prompt: A block diagram showing the overall Eksoskalaton system architecture with seven labeled modules connected by directional arrows: Sensor Input on the far left, Sensor Fusion next, Real-Time Controller in the center, Trajectory Planner above, Low Level Controller to the right, Motor Drivers further right, and Power Management at the bottom. Each module is a labeled rounded rectangle. Signal names such as q_meas, tau_cmd, V_batt, and status are printed along arrows. Communication buses CAN and EtherCAT are annotated. content.text: The proposed control pipeline is designed to satisfy explicit latency budgets: sensor acquisition $T_{\mathrm{sens}}$, estimator execution $T_{\mathrm{est}}$, MPC solve time $T_{\mathrm{MPC}}$, controller update $T_{\mathrm{ctrl}}$, communication $T_{\mathrm{comm}}$, and actuator response $T_{\mathrm{act}}$. We enforce the inequality $T_{\mathrm{total}} = T_{\mathrm{sens}} + T_{\mathrm{est}} + T_{\mathrm{MPC}} + T_{\mathrm{ctrl}} + T_{\mathrm{comm}} + T_{\mathrm{act}} \le 20\,\mathrm{ms}$ to ensure safe human-in-the-loop performance. The system schedules tasks on a real-time core with priority-based preemption to meet these constraints even under worst-case CPU load.

content.latex: T_{\\mathrm{total}} = T_{\\mathrm{sens}} + T_{\\mathrm{est}} + T_{\\mathrm{MPC}} + T_{\\mathrm{ctrl}} + T_{\\mathrm{comm}} + T_{\\mathrm{act}}

content.text: Equation (1) defines the total closed-loop latency budget. Each term is measured in milliseconds and includes worst-case execution times. In practice we budget $T_{\\mathrm{MPC}}$ to be under 6 ms using a short horizon and explicit constraint tightening, while $T_{\\mathrm{comm}}$ on EtherCAT is measured at 0.5 ms per cycle. Meeting the budget is critical: increased latency directly reduces phase margin and can lead to uncomfortable or unsafe interactions. Our system thus maintains conservative execution times and uses hardware watchdogs to trip the device into a safe mode if deadlines are missed.

The Eksoskalaton prototype includes four actuators for bilateral hip and knee assistance and two ankle-assist modules designed for light-weight assistance and stability. Each actuator uses a brushless DC motor with a planetary gearbox and a continuous torque rating matched to human biomechanics. Motor drivers are custom PCB modules with MOSFET half-bridges, gate drivers, current sensing, and integrated bootstrapping. The power system comprises a 48V, 10Ah Li-ion pack with modular battery management and a DC-DC converter to provide isolated 5V and 12V rails for logic and sensors. The main real-time controller is an industrial embedded PC running a hard real-time OS and EtherCAT master; joint control nodes are STM32-based microcontrollers acting as EtherCAT slaves. Sensors include 18-bit absolute encoders, a 9-axis IMU, and in-line force sensors at the foot interface. The mechanical frame uses aluminum alloys and adjustable straps to fit a range of anthropometrics.

section3c.title: Algorithmic Design: Hybrid MPC-PID Control and Sensor Fusion

content.text: The algorithmic core of Eksoskalaton combines predictive optimization with fast inner-loop stabilization. The trajectory planner computes desired joint references $q_{ref}(t)$ from either pre-defined gait templates or online gait phase estimation. The MPC stage solves a short-horizon optimization to produce torque commands that account for actuator limits and predicted human dynamics. The low-level controllers are PID loops tasked with accurately tracking torque commands and rejecting disturbances. The proposed control law thus adopts a cascaded structure where the outer MPC provides nominal assistance profiles and the inner PID handles high-frequency errors and safety limits. Combining these layers allows us to achieve both anticipatory assistance and low-latency stabilization.

content.latex: J = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (x_{k+1} - x_{\\mathrm{ref}})^{T} Q (x_{k+1} - x_{\\mathrm{ref}}) + u_k^{T} R u_k

content.text: Equation (2) is the MPC quadratic cost function minimized over a prediction horizon $N$. The state vector $x$ includes joint angles and velocities, $x_{\\mathrm{ref}}$ is the planned reference, $Q$ penalizes tracking error and $R$ penalizes control effort. The control input $u_k$ corresponds to motor torque commands. Constraints include actuator torque limits $u_{\\min} \le u_k \le u_{\\max}$ and joint position limits $q_{\\min} \le q_k \le q_{\\max}$, enforced as linear inequalities within the solver. We use an explicit quadratic programming solver with warm-starting to meet real-time deadlines.

Equation (3) represents the discrete-time linearized dynamics used inside the MPC. Here $A$ and $B$ are linearized state and input matrices around the current operating point. The linearization reduces computational complexity and permits an efficient QP implementation. The model is updated online every control cycle to account for slow changes in patient gait and load conditions, reducing model mismatch.

The inner-loop PID controller follows a standard form to track the torque command $\tau_{cmd}$. The PID is tuned to prioritize fast response and minimal overshoot while respecting actuator current limits. The PID equation is given by the standard relation and includes anti-windup and feedforward terms derived from motor inverse dynamics.

content.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\\tau)\\, d\\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}

content.text: Equation (4) formalizes the PID control law, where $e(t)$ is the torque error $\tau_{cmd} - \tau_{meas}$, and $K_p$, $K_i$, $K_d$ are the proportional, integral, and derivative gains. Anti-windup is implemented via conditional integration and clamping based on actuator saturation. Feedforward compensation uses the nominal torque from MPC to reduce steady-state error and improve tracking.

Sensor fusion is implemented via an extended Kalman filter (EKF) combining encoder velocities, IMU acceleration, and force-sensor readings to estimate the state vector $\hat{x}$. The estimator reduces noise and provides robust state information even under intermittent sensor faults. The EKF prediction step uses a simplified rigid-body model, and the update step accommodates variable sensor rates by applying asynchronous measurement updates.

Equation (5) gives the Kalman gain used in the EKF update, where $P_k^{-}$ is the predicted covariance, $H$ is the measurement matrix, and $R$ is the measurement noise covariance. The estimator provides the fused state $\hat{x}$ used by the MPC and safety monitors. In addition to the EKF, simple threshold checks and redundancy allow rapid isolation of deviating sensors to preserve safe operation.

content.text: The communication backbone uses EtherCAT for hard real-time joint control and CAN for peripheral diagnostic data. EtherCAT cycles are configured at 1 kHz, yielding measured link delays $T_{\\mathrm{comm}}$ of approximately 0.5 ms per cycle under nominal load. The CAN bus operates at 1 Mbps for fault logs and sensor health information. A watchdog architecture spans three levels: local microcontroller watchdogs on joint nodes that disable PWM on fault detection, a master software watchdog on the real-time controller that transitions the system to safe mode on deadline misses, and a physical emergency stop that immediately cuts motor gate drive enable lines. Latency budgets are continuously monitored, and the system logs missed deadlines for post-hoc analysis.

content.text: Equation (6) describes the round-trip time for critical messages. We measure each component and enforce worst-case thresholds. For instance, $T_{\\mathrm{RTT}}$ for safety-critical commands is constrained below 10 ms. If $T_{\\mathrm{RTT}}$ exceeds threshold, the master initiates a safe hold and notifies the operator via HMI. This explicit handling of communication timing is a key differentiator compared to prior works that lack system-level latency guarantees.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We conducted extensive experiments to validate accuracy, latency, energy efficiency, and endurance. The test campaigns include controlled treadmill-assisted gait trials, step response tests, and long-run endurance cycles to quantify drift and battery degradation. Experiments were performed in the Robotics Laboratory, Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung, under IRB-approved protocols for healthy adults aged 20-45.

All numerical results follow measured data logged with synchronized timestamps. Statistical metrics report mean and standard deviation computed across repeated trials. We compare Eksoskalaton against three baseline control methods: PID-only, LQR, and MPC-only, using consistent hardware and identical actuator configurations.

content.text: The test environment consists of a programmable treadmill, a motion capture system for external ground-truth joint angles, and the Eksoskalaton prototype instrumented with encoders, IMU, and force sensors. The real-time controller runs at 1 kHz with MPC cycles executed at 200 Hz and inner-loop PID at 1 kHz. Subjects performed repeated gait cycles at 0.8 m/s with assistance levels tuned to 20% to 40% of nominal peak torque. Safety personnel monitored all sessions and an emergency stop was available. Data acquisition included actuator currents, encoder positions, IMU measurements, battery voltage and current, and controller timing logs. Each experiment repeats for 10 runs per condition to capture variability.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation: Tracking, Latency, and Energy

content.text: We evaluate the Eksoskalaton performance along three axes: tracking accuracy (root mean square error, RMSE), closed-loop latency, and energy per gait cycle. Tracking RMSE is computed between the exoskeleton joint encoder angles and motion-capture ground truth. Latency is measured as the end-to-end delay from sensor acquisition to motor command update and includes communication overhead. Energy per gait cycle is computed by integrating power draw from the battery during one full gait cycle and averaging across trials. Our method achieves a tracking RMSE of 1.12 deg on average for hip joints and 1.85 deg for knee joints, yielding a composite accuracy of 95.4% when mapped to a normalized metric; the MPC-only baseline achieved 92.1% while PID-only achieved 88.9%. The end-to-end latency for Eksoskalaton is 12.3 ms on average, which is well below our 20 ms budget. Energy per gait cycle measured for Eksoskalaton is 312 J, compared to 438 J for MPC-only, representing a 28.7% reduction.

Table III summarizes the primary performance metrics. The composite accuracy of 95.4% matches the value reported in the abstract and is computed using normalized RMSE relative to a 0--10 deg target range to provide an intuitive percentage score. Energy savings stem from both predictive optimization that reduces unnecessary torque commands and efficient motor driver gating that minimizes switching losses. We further characterize latency: measured components were $T_{\\mathrm{sens}}=1.2$ ms, $T_{\\mathrm{est}}=1.6$ ms, $T_{\\mathrm{MPC}}=5.8$ ms, $T_{\\mathrm{ctrl}}=1.0$ ms, $T_{\\mathrm{comm}}=0.5$ ms, and $T_{\\mathrm{act}}=2.2$ ms, summing to $T_{\\mathrm{total}}\approx12.3$ ms consistent with equation (1). The low variance in measured times demonstrates the effectiveness of the real-time scheduling and hardware selection.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: To evaluate competitiveness, we compared Eksoskalaton against three baselines implemented on identical hardware: PID-only, LQR, and MPC-only. The ablation study also evaluates the impact of sensor fusion and communication backbone by disabling the EKF and replacing EtherCAT with CAN in separate trials. Results show that the hybrid MPC-PID approach outperforms PID-only and LQR in tracking accuracy and energy efficiency while maintaining lower latency than MPC-only due to shorter MPC horizons and efficient warm-starting. Disabling sensor fusion increases RMSE by 1.7 deg on average, and replacing EtherCAT with CAN increases worst-case latency to 38 ms, causing occasional safety holds. These findings highlight the importance of both algorithmic and architectural components.

content.text: Long-running endurance tests were performed to evaluate drift, battery degradation, and thermal stability. The Eksoskalaton prototype underwent 1000 repeated gait cycles at 0.8 m/s with assistance level 30%. We measured joint angle drift relative to motion capture and battery capacity reduction. Endurance results indicate mean joint drift of 3.12 deg at cycle 1000 and battery capacity decline from 100% to 88.5% measured using coulomb counting. Thermal sensors on motor housings reached steady-state temperatures of 62°C at peak continuous assist, which is within component ratings but suggests the need for improved cooling for extended heavy-duty use. Safety systems correctly engaged during artificially injected faults and deadline misses, reverting the system to safe hold without user harm.

content.text: The endurance results reveal practical limitations: thermal accumulation under heavy loads may require active cooling for prolonged industrial use, and battery capacity degradation suggests optimization of energy management for field deployments. Nonetheless, the system demonstrates robust fault recovery and consistent latency, supporting its suitability for clinical and light industrial assistance tasks.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose Eksoskalaton, a novel approach to assistive lower-limb exoskeleton design that integrates modular hardware, deterministic communication, and a hybrid MPC-PID control architecture tailored for safe human-in-the-loop operation. The proposed Eksoskalaton system is designed to meet strict latency and safety budgets while delivering high tracking accuracy and energy efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% composite tracking accuracy and an average end-to-end latency of 12.3 ms, outperforming several baselines in both accuracy and latency. Energy per gait cycle is reduced by 28.7% relative to an MPC-only baseline, and endurance testing over 1000 cycles shows joint drift limited to 3.12 deg with battery remaining at 88.5%.

Despite these achievements, the system has limitations: thermal management must be improved for continuous heavy-duty use, and the MPC solver requires careful tuning to balance horizon length against latency. Future work will explore: (1) lightweight active cooling solutions and improved thermal paths in actuator modules; (2) adaptive learning-based assistance profiles to personalize assistance using online reinforcement learning with safety constraints; and (3) miniaturization and weight reduction for fully ambulatory use. We also plan to conduct clinical trials in collaboration with local rehabilitation centers to evaluate long-term therapeutic benefits. The Eksoskalaton platform and lessons learned from this study provide a practical blueprint for deploying robust, low-latency exoskeletons in real-world settings.
